title: MIFARE Ultralight C — HF Chip Technical Encyclopedia (Memory, 3DES Auth, Counters, Deployment)
kicker: MIFARE Ultralight C (MF0ICU2) / Ultralight EV1 / Ultralight Nano Reference
summary: MIFARE Ultralight C (NXP MF0ICU2) is the low-cost, paper-ticket-oriented HF 13.56 MHz chip that brought triple-DES authentication to single-use and short-life credentials. Shipping since 2008, it extends the original Ultralight architecture with 144 bytes of user memory, 3DES mutual authentication (16-byte key, based on NIST SP 800-67 Triple DES), a one-way 24-bit counter for event-ticket validation, and the ISO 14443-A Part 3 layer. Used in event tickets, transport single-ride tickets, limited-edition gift cards, and any application where a paper-substrate HF chip with tamper-resistant authentication is needed.
heroPoints: Paper-first form factor — the Ultralight family is the standard chip for printed event tickets, transit single-rides, and NFC business cards printed on paper/PVC. Ultralight C adds 3DES to the mix: 48 bytes more user memory than the original Ultralight, plus a proper cryptographic auth handshake that makes cloning meaningfully harder than raw Ultralight.

3DES mutual authentication — 16-byte (112-bit effective) key authenticated via a two-step challenge/response. NIST SP 800-67 Triple-DES with the 3-key variant. Not as strong as AES-128, but considerably stronger than Classic's CRYPTO1 and the original Ultralight's UID-only binding. Adequate for short-validity event tickets.

One-way 24-bit counter — a hardware-enforced monotonic counter that only increments. Perfect for event-ticket validation (counter bumps on entry scan), single-ride transit tickets, and anti-replay tokens. The counter cannot be decremented by any command, giving downstream systems a hard audit trail.

sections.title: Family and part numbers
bullets: MIFARE Ultralight C — NXP part number MF0ICU2. The 3DES-capable variant. 192 bytes total memory, of which 144 bytes are user-writable. Launched 2008, still in volume production as of 2026.

MIFARE Ultralight (original) — MF0ICU1. 64 bytes total, 48 bytes user. No crypto. Was the original paper-ticket chip for transit and events; mostly superseded by Ultralight EV1 or NTAG213 in new deployments.

MIFARE Ultralight EV1 — MF0UL11 / MF0UL21. Launched 2012. 48-byte and 128-byte user-memory variants. Adds per-block lock, 32-bit one-way counter, and an Originality Signature (ECDSA-based tag-authentication using an NXP key) for anti-counterfeit. No 3DES — EV1 is sold as a drop-in replacement for the original Ultralight plus NTAG21x-style features rather than as an Ultralight C successor.
MIFARE Ultralight Nano — MF0UN00. 40-byte user memory, 'bare-bones' chip for single-use paper tickets at the lowest possible cost. No crypto. 2017 launch.

NTAG21x relationship — NTAG213 / NTAG215 / NTAG216 are a parallel product family aimed at general-purpose NFC tagging rather than ticketing. Shared 14443-A layer but different command sets; NTAG21x has its own Fast Read and dynamic-URL features that Ultralight does not.

Counterfeit watch — authentic Ultralight C returns ATQA = 0x0044 and SAK = 0x00 (ISO 14443-3 cascade continues beyond the first anti-collision round). The GET_VERSION command (0x60) on Ultralight EV1 and newer returns NXP manufacturer ID 0x04; pre-GET_VERSION Ultralight C identifies via page 2-3 header data.

sections.title: Memory architecture
bullets: Ultralight C total layout — 48 pages of 4 bytes each = 192 bytes total. Pages 0-3 hold UID, BCC, internal config. Pages 4-39 are user-writable data (144 bytes). Pages 40-43 hold the 3DES key and lock bits. Pages 44-47 are configuration (counter, key config).

User data — 144 bytes starting at page 4. Typical NDEF-formatted Ultralight C carries a URL NDEF record (for NFC tap-to-web), or a transit/ticket-specific binary format with ticket type, validity window, and digital signature.
UID and serial — 7-byte unique UID returned via the 14443-A anti-collision layer. Pages 0-1 contain the UID bytes; this is factory-programmed and cannot be rewritten.

Lock bytes — pages 2 and 40 contain static and dynamic lock bits. Once a page is locked, its data becomes read-only. Block-level lock is the mechanism used to commit a ticket after initial personalization so it cannot be re-used or re-programmed.

One-way 16-bit counter (EV1) / 24-bit counter (C) — hardware monotonic counter. Readable at any time without authentication. Writable via INCREMENT_COUNTER (0xA5) command, which increments the counter by a reader-supplied delta. Cannot be decremented or reset.

3DES key storage — the 16-byte 3DES key lives in pages 44-47, write-only after initial personalization. Key-set via WRITE commands during factory/issuance; after the configuration bit is set, the key pages return 0x00 on read but still participate in the 3DES authentication math.

Write endurance — 10,000 write cycles per page (significantly lower than Classic or NTAG21x). Data retention ≥ 5 years. These numbers reflect the low-cost-paper positioning; Ultralight C is not for long-lived or frequently-updated credentials.

sections.title: 3DES authentication protocol
bullets: 3DES — Triple DES with three 56-bit keys (K1, K2, K3) for 112 bits effective security. NIST SP 800-67 Rev. 2 compliant. Per NIST SP 800-131A, 3DES is deprecated for new US-government systems as of 2024 but remains acceptable for legacy interoperability through 2030.

Mutual-authentication handshake — 2-message protocol. (1) Reader sends AUTHENTICATE (0x1A) with key-slot selector. (2) Tag generates nonce RndB, encrypts it with the 3DES key, returns enc(RndB). (3) Reader decrypts RndB, generates its own RndA, concatenates RndA + RndB' (RndB left-rotated by one byte), encrypts, sends to tag. (4) Tag decrypts, verifies its RndB' matches, returns enc(RndA') as confirmation.

Session key derivation — after successful mutual auth, both sides derive a session key from RndA + RndB. Subsequent Read and Write commands on protected pages use this session key for MAC verification and optional encryption.

Anti-cloning vs anti-counterfeit — Ultralight C's 3DES provides anti-cloning for the key material: an attacker cannot recover the 3DES key by observing the handshake. Does NOT provide anti-counterfeit against clones with the same key (all cards in a batch typically share a key); add the EV1 Originality Signature if per-chip authenticity verification is needed.
Performance — the 3DES exchange adds ~20-40 ms to each reader tap compared to non-authenticated Ultralight. For event-turnstile throughput this is inside the acceptable latency budget.

Key management — a single Ultralight C key is shared across the issuance batch. For event-ticket applications this is fine (ticket-by-ticket diversification is achieved via the serial + UID). For higher-security uses, diversify the 3DES key per-card using a master-key-and-UID KDF; see NXP AN12196 for the recipe.

sections.title: One-way counter and ticket validation
bullets: 24-bit counter on Ultralight C / 16-bit counter per-key on EV1 — hardware monotonic increment-only counter. Starting value zero, max 2^24 - 1 (~16.7 M). Cannot be decremented or reset.

Read without auth — READ_COUNTER (0x39) returns the current value without requiring authentication. Useful for reader-only verification of ticket state before the 3DES auth adds its tax to the transaction.

Increment command — INCREMENT_COUNTER (0xA5) with a 3-byte delta. The tag adds the delta to the counter and persists. Default delta = 1 for a simple ticket-used bump. Implementers can choose larger deltas for multi-ride tickets (burn 4 units on entry to a 4-ride pass).

Typical ticket flow — at issuance, the ticket is personalized with counter = 0 and locked. At the entry gate, the reader (a) reads the counter, (b) verifies ticket validity server-side, (c) increments counter by 1, (d) displays green light. Re-entry attempts find counter > 0 and are rejected.

Anti-replay security — because the counter is monotonic, a captured authentication transcript cannot be replayed to gain entry; the authentication includes the counter value which will have advanced. This is Ultralight C's main appeal over the original Ultralight for single-use event tickets.

Counter rollover — at 2^24 events per card, the counter cannot be reset. For single-use tickets this is not a concern. For multi-use memberships (e.g., 1000-use gym cards) this exceeds lifetime event count.

sections.title: ISO 14443-A Part 3 compliance and RF
bullets: Ultralight family implements ISO/IEC 14443-A Parts 1-3. Like Classic, it does not implement ISO 14443-4 (T=CL transmission protocol). Reader interacts via raw 14443-A frames wrapping Ultralight-specific command opcodes (READ, WRITE, AUTHENTICATE, COMPATIBILITY_WRITE, INCREMENT_COUNTER, READ_COUNTER, GET_VERSION).
ATQA / SAK — ATQA = 0x0044 for Ultralight (all variants). SAK = 0x00, indicating cascade continues to 7-byte UID. UID bytes are returned via the anti-collision sequence.

Command opcodes — READ (0x30, returns 16 bytes starting at specified page), WRITE (0xA2, writes 4 bytes to a page), GET_VERSION (0x60, returns chip-identification bytes on EV1+), AUTHENTICATE (0x1A, Ultralight C), READ_SIG (0x3C, EV1 originality signature).

RF range — 0-8 cm typical on ID-1 card antenna, shorter on paper ticket antenna (30-40 mm × 20 mm typical loop). Paper-ticket antennas are aggressively miniaturized to fit on credit-card-size paper; read range reflects this.

Compatibility — every NFC phone, turnstile, access reader, and library kiosk shipped since 2015 supports Ultralight at the 14443-A level. Ultralight C's 3DES exchange requires reader-side software; not all readers implement it, but major transit and event vendors do.

sections.title: Commercial deployments and application fit
bullets: Event tickets — concerts, sports matches, conferences. Paper or PVC tickets with Ultralight C print at ~€0.10-0.20 per unit at volume; the 3DES gives enough cloning resistance to deter opportunistic counterfeiting. Monotonic counter enables single-use validation. Volume deployers: Ticketmaster, large festival operators, national-league sports clubs.

Transit single-ride tickets — paper tickets for subway and bus single rides. Original Ultralight dominated this segment 2004-2015; Ultralight C has grown share where single-ride revenue warrants tamper-resistance. City-scale deployments exist in the Netherlands, Japan, and several German cities.

Gift cards and promotional tags — limited-edition campaigns where a short-lived NFC tap experience is sufficient. 144 bytes of user memory accommodates a URL + small payload (campaign ID, one-time token).

NFC business cards (legacy) — Ultralight C was used in early NFC business card products 2012-2018; mostly displaced by NTAG213/215/216 which have better sensitivity, more memory, and the modern NTAG Fast Read for snappier phone taps. A few premium card vendors still spec Ultralight C for its 3DES.

Museum and venue visitor credentials — day-pass credentials for museums, theme-park day-pass wristbands. Ultralight C's 3DES + counter fits the use case: authenticated entry + one-way-per-turnstile logging.

Where Ultralight C is NOT the right choice — permanent access credentials (use Plus or DESFire for crypto agility + file system), high-read-cycle applications (write endurance is 10k vs 100k on Classic), and applications needing read-only tag-authenticity proof (the Originality Signature is on EV1, not C). Also not suitable for new-greenfield NDEF-only NFC stickers where NTAG213 is cheaper and has Fast Read.

Migration options — for applications where 3DES is becoming inadequate (2030+ NIST deprecation), the migration path is Ultralight EV1 (drops 3DES but adds signature) or NTAG424 DNA (adds AES-128 + SUN cryptographic URL) depending on whether the replacement workflow needs symmetric-auth or dynamic-URL proofing.

sections.title: NXP and ISO reference documents
bullets: NXP MF0ICU2 Product Data Sheet — the canonical Ultralight C reference. Memory map, command opcodes, 3DES handshake state diagram, electrical characterization.
NXP AN11340 — MIFARE Ultralight feature comparison. Covers Ultralight / Ultralight C / Ultralight EV1 / Ultralight Nano differences across memory, commands, and security features.
NXP AN12196 — MIFARE diversification keys. Includes the key-derivation-from-UID recipe used by production issuance systems to assign a unique 3DES key per card.
ISO/IEC 14443-3:2018 — air-interface standard Ultralight implements.
NIST SP 800-67 Rev. 2 — Triple DES block cipher specification. The 3DES variant used by Ultralight C is 'TDEA-EDE3' (Encrypt-Decrypt-Encrypt with 3 independent keys) per this document.

NIST SP 800-131A Rev. 2 — crypto-deprecation guidance. Deprecates 3DES for new US-government systems in 2024; allows legacy interoperability through 2030. Governs migration planning for Ultralight C-based installations.

faq.question: Is Ultralight C's 3DES still secure enough in 2026?
faq.answer: For short-validity event tickets and single-use transit rides, yes. NIST SP 800-131A deprecates 3DES for new US-government systems as of 2024 but permits legacy interoperability through 2030. Ultralight C tickets typically have a validity window measured in hours to days, so they age out faster than 3DES's deprecation window. For long-validity credentials (multi-year membership cards, building access), migrate to NTAG424 DNA or DESFire EV3 with AES-128.

faq.question: When should I pick Ultralight C vs NTAG213?
faq.answer: Pick Ultralight C when you need 3DES authentication (anti-cloning for event tickets), a one-way counter (single-use validation), or compatibility with an installed base of Ultralight-aware transit/event readers. Pick NTAG213 when you need general-purpose NFC tagging (tap-to-URL, NDEF-based campaigns), faster reads (NTAG Fast Read), or a unique per-chip Originality Signature (NTAG213 has it; Ultralight C does not). Per-unit cost is similar at volume.

faq.question: Can the one-way counter on Ultralight C be reset or decremented?
faq.answer: No. The counter is hardware-enforced monotonic; there is no command to decrement or reset it. This is by design — for single-use event tickets the counter is the anti-replay mechanism. If the ticket is scanned erroneously and the counter bumps, the fix is operational (issue a replacement ticket) rather than protocol-level (un-bump the counter). Plan your ticket issuance with enough counter headroom for expected misreads.

faq.question: How many key slots does Ultralight C support?
faq.answer: One. Ultralight C stores a single 16-byte 3DES key (pages 44-47). For multi-application credentials needing multiple access domains, use MIFARE Plus (multiple sector keys) or DESFire EV3 (file-system with per-file AES keys). Ultralight C's single-key model is appropriate for single-purpose tickets and single-application credentials.

faq.question: Is there an 'Ultralight D' with AES?
faq.answer: Not under that name. NXP's AES-capable Ultralight-positioned chip is NTAG424 DNA (NT4H2421), which adds AES-128, SUN (Secure Unique NFC) message format, and CMAC-based tag authentication. If you were planning an 'Ultralight C successor with AES', NTAG424 DNA is the recommended chip.

faq.question: What's the typical write endurance of Ultralight C in laundry or outdoor deployments?
faq.answer: Write endurance is 10,000 cycles per page — roughly 10× less than Classic or NTAG21x. For deployments that write frequently (counter-bump per day, per-use status updates) this is a real constraint. A card written once at issuance and only read thereafter (typical ticket pattern) will outlast its validity window. For frequently-written credentials, choose Ultralight EV1 (100k cycles) or DESFire.

faq.question: Does Ultralight C work with iPhone and Android for NDEF taps?
faq.answer: Yes. iPhone (iOS 11+) and all recent Android phones read Ultralight C as a standard NFC Forum Type 2 tag. NDEF-formatted user memory is accessible to stock wallet and browser apps via standard NFC tap-to-launch flows. The 3DES authentication layer is NOT exposed to stock phone apps; applications requiring the 3DES handshake need a custom app using the NFC APIs (Core NFC on iOS, android.nfc on Android) to drive the authenticate command directly.
